assessment.nobel_worthiness: A theory-led prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle, followed by experimental discovery of correlated-insulator and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opened the moire-materials field. It is a clear case of a prediction matched by nature, which I value, and its originality and downstream impact (twistronics, fractional Chern states, a new platform for correlated physics) are large.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum-model prediction and the Cao et al. experiments led by Jarillo-Herrero are decisive; the three credited names form a clean theory-plus-experiment configuration. Experimental first-author contributions (e.g. Yuan Cao) and earlier twisted-graphene theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) raise allocation questions that I cannot resolve from the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduced the correlated and superconducting phases within a few years, so the core observation is robust. Interpretation of the superconducting mechanism is still debated, but the discovery itself is mature enough and timely.
uncertainties: Whether the pairing mechanism will settle and affect how the prize citation is framed.
Fairness to early theory contributors and the first author of the experiments not in the credited set.
My recollection of the detailed priority history is from general knowledge, not independently verified here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned the foundations of quantum mechanics (no-cloning, entanglement, Bell tests) into a protocol and then into satellite-scale and networked practice. The BB84 idea is conceptually original and has had lasting impact on quantum information science, and experimental demonstrations are tangible discoveries rather than only constructions.
assessment.attribution: BB84 by Bennett and Brassard is the foundational contribution; Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is a separate and arguably independent conception; Pan led large-scale experimental realisation (satellite links, long-distance entanglement distribution). Only three of the four credited names can be chosen, and omitting Ekert is a real cost, so the configuration is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Protocols date from the 1980s and 1990s and are experimentally realised and widely commercialised; long-distance and satellite demonstrations are recent but replicated in part. Recognition is timely given the 2022 prize on entanglement tests.
uncertainties: Ekert versus Pan for the third place; Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not in the credited set.
Practical security (device imperfections, side channels) is not a physics-discovery issue but may weigh on committee perception.
Overlap with the 2022 Bell-test prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The IceCube detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, then the association of TXS 0506+056 and of the Galactic plane with neutrino emission, opened neutrino astronomy at TeV-PeV energies. This is a genuine discovery from nature that bears on cosmic-ray origins, and it is a clear fit to a prize centred on discoveries.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the IceCube concept and Karle was a leading figure in the construction and the experiment; the credited pair is small but the discovery is a large-collaboration result, and AMANDA/IceCube leadership (and others such as the spokespersons) may complicate the picture. Two names are supportable but credit within the collaboration is not fully resolved.
assessment.maturity: Diffuse flux confirmed by multiple analysis channels at high significance; source identification is still limited to a few objects and the picture of the main sources remains evolving. Recognition may be somewhat early for the astrophysical-source part but the detection itself is established.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should rest on the diffuse-flux detection or on source identification.
Collaboration credit and the roles of other IceCube leaders.
Unresolved origin of most of the observed flux.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea, reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and make precision tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and relativistic geodesy possible. It is an important and clear measurement advance with broad impact, as a successor to earlier frequency-metrology prizes.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice-clock concept and demonstrated the early clock; Ye's group pushed accuracy and many-body physics in strontium clocks. Both are decisive; other groups (Lemonde, Gill, Hinkley/Ludlow, Hollberg) overlap, so a two-person prize is plausible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have confirmed performance and a redefinition of the second is under discussion, so the field is mature; the prize may be seen as an extension of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap with ion-clock work and prior prizes.
Whether the committee judges the achievement an invention or a discovery.
Priority and credit among clock groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and its experimental realisation (Blatt and others) established a leading platform for quantum computation, with entangled-state creation and algorithms on ion chains. The work shows a theory proposal being implemented, which I find a strong pattern, though it follows the 2012 prize for single-system quantum control.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the 1995 scheme; Blatt led major experimental implementations, while Wineland's group (already a laureate), Monroe and others were also decisive. The credited trio is coherent but the experimental part is shared across several groups, so allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Over thirty years of progress with many independent confirmations; commercial-scale machines exist. The case is mature but quantum-computing hardware prizes may compete in timing with superconducting and neutral-atom platforms.
uncertainties: Monroe's and Wineland's roles; the near-duplicate candidate B035 with the same names.
Whether recognition should be for platform-specific work or for the broader quantum-computing foundations.
2025 prize on superconducting circuits may influence timing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Direct horizon-scale images of the M87* and Sgr A* shadows provide a striking test of general relativity in the strong-field regime and confirm the existence of supermassive compact objects. As someone working on black-hole physics, I value the observational clues, though the test of GR is presently of limited precision.
assessment.attribution: Doeleman led the EHT VLBI effort, Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept, and Moran contributed to the mm-VLBI foundations; yet the EHT is a collaboration of hundreds, and the key imaging and analysis contributions (e.g. Bouman, Broderick, Loeb, Narayan, Johnson) are not in the credited set, so allocation is genuinely problematic.
assessment.maturity: Two sources have been imaged, with polarisation follow-up; independent reanalysis exists but the dataset is single-collaboration by nature. Recognition is arguably somewhat early but would not be unreasonable.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration attribution and the one-to-three-person constraint.
Limited precision for testing alternatives to Kerr and the 2020 black-hole prize.
Image reconstruction dependence on priors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators by Kane and Mele, followed by experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells and then 3D materials, created a major branch of condensed matter physics. It is a theory-then-experiment story of high originality and wide impact, with some overlap with the 2016 topological-phase prize.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 theory; Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state, following Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's proposal. Bernevig, Zhang (deceased), Hughes, Fu, Hasan and Moore all made decisive contributions, so the credited configuration is contested; I choose theory plus first experiment and leave Hasan out.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed by many independent groups, including ARPES on 3D topological insulators; the field is mature and the time since 2005-2007 makes recognition due.
uncertainties: Overlap between B040 and B023 and the unresolved role of Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan.
Relationship to the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Whether the prize should split between 2D and 3D discoveries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Metal-halide perovskite solar cells rose from a few percent to over 25 percent efficiency in a decade, a remarkable materials discovery with strong practical interest. The underlying physics (defect tolerance, long carrier lifetimes) is interesting, but I weigh this lower as physics than the other candidates, and stability is a concern.
assessment.attribution: Miyasaka reported the first perovskite-sensitised cell in 2009, Park produced the solid-state cell of 2012 with much higher efficiency, and Snaith demonstrated the meso-superstructured and planar devices; the three form a plausible trio, though others (Grätzel, Seok) also made decisive contributions.
assessment.maturity: Efficiency records are reproduced widely, but long-term stability and commercial viability are not settled, so the field may be too young for a prize.
uncertainties: Role of Grätzel and Seok, who are not in the credited set.
Stability and toxicity could mean recognition is premature.
Physics versus chemistry/engineering in prize classification.
